title: Open LLM Leaderboard (archived) and its evaluation-results datasets
institution: Hugging Face
access: free download; Space archived read-only, result files remain openly downloadable on the Hub
verification: Dataset file viewer read at origin (huggingface.co/datasets/open-llm-leaderboard/results) 2026-11-05: per-model lm-evaluation-harness results for MMLU-Pro (5-shot, 12,032 samples), BBH (3-shot), MATH-Hard (4-shot), GPQA, MuSR and IFEval (0-shot), with model_num_parameters, dtype and total_evaluation_time_seconds fields. Archived status and v2 benchmark suite corroborated via WebSearch (retirement discussion #1135; 200+ community leaderboards remain). The Space page itself rendered only a stub.
relevance: An archive of hundreds of open-weights LLM evaluations run through the Open LLM Leaderboard v2 harness, with full per-task configs, sample counts and raw accuracy metrics for MMLU-Pro, BBH, MATH-Hard, GPQA, MuSR and IFEval. Maintained by Hugging Face's open-llm-leaderboard organisation; submissions were disabled and the Space retired in 2025, but the results datasets remain downloadable and 200+ community leaderboards continue on the Hub. A learner can reproduce pre-retirement open-model comparisons or study how composite leaderboards were built. Limits: results stop at retirement, and licence terms sit on each dataset card rather than the viewer.

title: Artificial Analysis - independent model intelligence, price and latency index
institution: Artificial Analysis (independent benchmarking company)
access: free web access; no public API; paid Optima / MicroEvals / Data Playground products
verification: Homepage read at origin 2026-11-05: Intelligence Index covers '28 of 722 models'; 'Cost per Task' and 'Time per Task' metrics; 'Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1 incorporates 9 evaluations' including AA-Briefcase v1.1 and Terminal-Bench 4.0; changelog shows 'Methodology updated - 3 Nov'; repeated 'No publicly available API' notices; evaluations 'measured independently by Artificial Analysis'; also Elo rankings for image/video/speech models and provider speed/latency/price comparisons.
relevance: Tracks 722 language, image, video and speech models against a composite Intelligence Index plus cost-per-task and time-per-task, and ranks API providers on speed, latency, price and endpoint accuracy - one of the few independent sources tying capability directly to price. Updated near-daily with a public changelog; benchmarks are measured in-house by Artificial Analysis. Free to browse, but there is no public API and some tools (Optima custom benchmarks) are commercial. Limits: methodology is proprietary, and the homepage does not surface GPU cloud pricing.

title: HELM - Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (open framework and leaderboards)
authors: Percy Liang et al., Stanford CRFM
institution: Center for Research on Foundation Models (CRFM), Stanford University
access: open source Apache-2.0; leaderboards free web; pip install crfm-helm
verification: GitHub repo read at origin (github.com/stanford-crfm/helm) 2026-11-05: Apache-2.0 licence; standardized benchmarks 'MMLU-Pro, GPQA, IFEval, WildBench'; metrics 'beyond accuracy (e.g. efficiency, bias, toxicity)'; 'HELM entered maintenance mode on June 1, 2026'; leaderboards HELM Capabilities, HELM Safety, VHELM, plus HEIM, MedHELM, The Mighty ToRR and 'classic'. The crfm.stanford.edu pages rendered only the title to the fetcher (JS-rendered site).
relevance: The longest-running transparent LLM evaluation effort: open-source code, public leaderboards for capabilities, safety and vision-language evaluation, and published scenario/metric results that made 'holistic' multi-metric evaluation standard practice. Maintained by Stanford CRFM under an Apache-2.0 licence. It entered maintenance mode on 1 June 2026, so it is best used as a stable historical archive and as tooling to run your own holistic evaluations rather than to track the newest frontier models. No scenario/model counts were visible at read time, so pull specifics from the leaderboard itself.

title: LMSYS-Chat-1M dataset + Chatbot Arena (LMArena) leaderboard
authors: Lianmin Zheng et al., LMSYS Org / UC Berkeley collaborators
institution: LMSYS Org (Large Model Systems Organization), UC Berkeley
access: gated download under the LMSYS-Chat-1M Dataset License Agreement; leaderboard free web
verification: HF dataset card read at origin 2026-11-05: 'one million real-world conversations with 25 state-of-the-art LLMs' collected April-August 2023 from the Vicuna demo and Chatbot Arena; 210,479 users; 154 languages; PII redacted via OpaquePrompts with placeholders like NAME_1; gated under a licence forbidding redistribution; unsafe conversations retained by design; citation Zheng et al. 2023 (arXiv:2309.11998). Arena leaderboard read at origin (lmarena.ai redirects to arena.ai) 2026-11-05: '374,173,556 Total Sessions'; category leaderboards for Agent, WebDev, Vision, Search, Image/Video; 'c Arena Intelligence 2026'; no explicit open-data release stated on the page.
relevance: Two complementary artefacts from crowd-sourced model evaluation: LMSYS-Chat-1M is the standard open corpus of one million real LLM conversations across 154 languages for studying how people actually prompt models, while the Arena leaderboard aggregates hundreds of millions of blind pairwise human votes into Elo-style rankings across text, vision, agents and web dev. The dataset is gated but research-friendly; PII redaction may affect quality and benchmark-contamination risks are documented. Limits: the leaderboard page does not state an open data dump, so researchers largely rely on the 2023 corpus and published methodology.

title: AI and Democratic Values Index (CAIDP Index)
authors: Center for AI and Digital Policy (2026 edition, ed. April Yoder)
institution: Center for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP), Washington DC
access: free PDF download; print version sold via booksellers
verification: Index 2026 page read at origin 2026-11-05: '90 countries' evaluated; '12 metrics established to assess alignment with democratic values'; published 'annually since 2021'; sixth edition spans 1,739 pages with 8,546 footnotes; press release (9 April 2026) names top-ranked countries 'Canada, Japan, the Netherlands, Norway, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom' and finds 'United States withdraws from global AI leadership'; prior editions 2020-2023 and 2025 linked.
relevance: Annual ranking and country profiles of how national AI policies align with democratic values, now covering 90 countries against 12 metrics, with editions back to 2020. Produced by CAIDP, a US non-profit drawing on thousands of its policy-clinic participants across 120+ countries; full reports are free PDFs (the 2026 edition alone is 1,739 pages). Useful next to OECD/MIT trackers because it scores implementation and rights alignment, not just legislation on the books. Limits: assessments reflect CAIDP's own normative framework and criteria.

title: Digital Policy Alert - activity tracker for digital and AI policy across jurisdictions
institution: SGEPT (St. Gallen Endowment for Technology Policy), Switzerland
access: free web under CC BY-NC 4.0; commercial use and API/MCP access under separate terms
verification: Homepage read at origin 2026-11-05: 'An SGEPT initiative'; 'Website content is available under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International licence'; 'Commercial use, and data delivered through our API or MCP server, are governed by our Terms'; Activity Tracker with Graph/Table views and a most-active-jurisdictions chart; examples span Australia, Saudi Arabia, Korea, EU, UK, US. Exact jurisdiction count not stated on the homepage.
relevance: A Swiss endowment-run tracker logging legislative and regulatory 'events' across digital policy areas - AI, data protection, online safety, cybersecurity - with country activity charts, upcoming-events feeds and an API. Website content is CC BY-NC 4.0; commercial use and API access carry separate terms. Valuable as a non-US/EU observatory that captures national-level developments (Korea's PIPA, Saudi PDPL, Australian securities guidance on AI) that OECD/MIT pages treat more thinly. Limit: it tracks the breadth of digital policy, not AI alone, so filter by policy area.

title: UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM) and the Global AI Ethics and Governance Observatory
institution: UNESCO
access: free; country RAM reports downloadable on UNESDOC
verification: Metadata only (lead): unesco.org returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch twice on 2026-11-05. Per WebSearch corroborations of UNESCO pages: RAM is the implementation tool of the 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of AI adopted by 193 Member States; 'more than 70 countries' have implemented or are implementing it (one source cites 77); assessments cover legal/regulatory, socio-cultural, economic, scientific/educational and technological/infrastructure dimensions; hosted under UNESCO's Global AI Ethics and Governance Observatory; country reports (e.g. Jamaica, Indonesia) on UNESDOC.
relevance: UNESCO's country-by-country implementation tracking for the Recommendation on the Ethics of AI: readiness assessments across law, socio-culture, economy, science/education and technology/infrastructure, with published country reports including Indonesia's. With 70+ countries having undertaken or undertaking RAM, it offers the broadest Global South coverage of any AI-governance readiness series, and RAM 2.0 is now in use. Free to read via UNESDOC, but UNESCO's site blocks some automated access, so plan manual browsing. A learner can compare official readiness diagnoses with what national AI strategies actually deliver.

title: AIAAIC Repository - AI, Algorithmic and Automation Incidents and Controversies
institution: AIAAIC (independent initiative)
access: free web repository, no login
verification: Repository listing read at origin (aiaaic.org) 2026-11-05: hundreds of linked incident entries (UK Post Office scandal, Uber AV fatality, Netherlands childcare benefits fraud automation, ImageNet and MS-Celeb-1M dataset controversies, ChatGPT/Gemini/Sora cases); companion 'AI algorithmic automation harms taxonomy' project linked. The About body did not render. Scale (1,500+ incidents compiled from 10,000+ media/research reports; ~3,754 records in recent citations) and founder Charlie Pownall per WebSearch corroborations (aiaaicalert.substack.com; OECD AI catalogue entry).
relevance: A free, browsable repository of real-world AI, algorithmic and automation incidents and controversies - from welfare-fraud automation and Post Office prosecutions to deepfakes and dataset scandals - compiled from media and research reports and used to build the collaborative AI harms taxonomy. It complements the AI Incident Database with a broader 'controversy' lens and heavier European/global coverage. Maintained independently alongside the AIAAIC Alert newsletter. Limits: entries are curated narrative case records rather than structured incident data, so quantitative analysis requires manual coding.

title: Deepfake-Eval-2024 - multi-modal in-the-wild deepfake detection benchmark
authors: Nikhil Chandra et al. (TrueMedia.org, University of Washington, Miraflow AI, Georgetown, Chung-Ang, Yonsei universities)
institution: TrueMedia.org / University of Washington et al.
access: gated on Hugging Face (manual approval); CC BY-SA 4.0; evaluation-only terms
verification: HF dataset card read at origin 2026-11-05: 44 hours video, 56.5 hours audio, 1,975 images from 88 website sources across 52 languages, manually labelled real/fake; licence 'cc-by-sa-4.0'; gated with approval and terms stating users 'may only use this dataset for evaluation' (training violates terms); access restricted to deepfake-detection work; stated limitations: skew toward 'English-speaking, light-skinned individuals from Western countries', small quantity of NSFW content, possible unconsented personal information.
relevance: The leading successor to academic deepfake sets like DFDC: real 2024 social-media deepfakes in audio, video and images across 52 languages, on which state-of-the-art detectors 'collapse' - now the standard stress test for in-the-wild detection. Built by TrueMedia.org with university partners; CC BY-SA 4.0 but gated, evaluation-only, restricted to deepfake-detection work. A learner can use it to test how well published detectors generalise beyond lab data. Stated limits: demographic skew toward Western English-speaking content and some NSFW or unconsented material.

title: O*NET occupational database (O*NET 31.0) - task, emerging-task and technology-skills files used for AI-exposure research
authors: Dan J. Putka, Nathaniel M. Voss, Phil Lewis (AI Impact review); USDOL/ETA and National Center for O*NET Development (database)
date: quarterly updates; O*NET 31.0 current (site updated 6 October 2026); AI Impact review June 2026
institution: U.S. Department of Labor ETA / National Center for O*NET Development (HumRRO for the review)
access: free download (Excel/CSV/JSON, SQL, RDF, web services); CC BY 4.0
verification: Database page read at origin 2026-11-05: O*NET 31.0; Task Statements 18,838 rows; Task Ratings 165,780 rows; Emerging Tasks 338 rows; Technology/Software Skills 31,821 rows; 'quarterly basis' updates; 'The O*NET 31.0 Database is available under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License'; sponsored by USDOL/ETA. Report page read at origin: 'Indexing the Impact of AI within the O*NET System' (June 2026, Putka/Voss/Lewis) reviews 19 AI-exposure studies, calls task-only measures 'potentially overstating AI's overall effect on occupations', and proposes a suite of 'potentially 16 AI impact indices'; CC BY 4.0; no ready-made score file.
relevance: The substrate for nearly every occupational AI-exposure index (Eloundou, Felten, Webb, ILO): hundreds of occupations with task statements, task ratings, emerging tasks and in-demand technology skills, updated quarterly and downloadable in multiple formats under CC BY 4.0. The June 2026 companion review critiques task-only AI-exposure measures and sketches 16 future AI impact indices built with LLM assistance - a roadmap for what DOL may release next. A learner can construct custom exposure measures; note that O*NET itself ships no ready-made AI score file.

title: Online Labour Index (OLI) - open index of online freelance labour supply and demand
date: 2016-2026 (automatic updates; newer OLI 2.0 at the Online Labour Observatory)
institution: Oxford Internet Institute, University of Oxford
access: open dataset on Figshare under CC-BY; old OLI version no longer actively maintained
verification: OLI page read at origin (ilabour.oii.ox.ac.uk) 2026-11-05: 'the first economic indicator that provides an online gig economy equivalent of conventional labour market statistics'; tracks 'all the projects/tasks posted on the five largest English-language online labour platforms, representing at least 70% of the market by traffic'; classified by occupation and employer country; results published as 'an automatically updated open data set' on Figshare under CC-BY; produced by Kassi & Lehdonvirta in the ERC-funded iLabour project; worker supplement since July 2017 on 'four major online labour platforms'. Note: onlinelabourobservatory.org served an invalid TLS certificate on 2026-11-05.
relevance: The standard time series for the online gig economy - a labour-market-statistics analogue built by scraping the five largest English-language freelance platforms, classified by occupation and employer country, with worker observations added since 2017. Open CC-BY dataset on Figshare, automatically updated; the newer OLI 2.0 lives at the Online Labour Observatory, whose domain had a TLS problem when checked. Useful for studying which countries supply AI-adjacent digital labour and how demand shifts. Limits: English-language platforms only, so much Global South supply is under-observed.

title: ENTSO-E Transparency Platform - European electricity generation, load, transmission and balancing data
authors: ENTSO-E (European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity)
institution: ENTSO-E, Brussels
access: free with registration; RESTful API; 2011-2014 data via 'Data Pre-5.1.15' section
verification: ENTSO-E page read at origin 2026-11-05: launched '5 January 2015' pursuant to Regulation (EU) No 543/2013 on submission and publication of data in electricity markets; mandatory for 'European Member State data providers and owners'; data on 'electricity generation, load, transmission and balancing'; collected from 'data providers such as TSOs, power exchanges or other qualified third parties'; predecessor voluntary site decommissioned March 2015. The platform UI (transparency.entsoe.eu) rendered an error screen to the fetcher; registration/API specifics restated only in platform documentation.
relevance: The legally mandated public record of Europe's power system: per-unit generation by fuel, load, cross-border flows and balancing data for EU/EEA transmission areas, with submission quality enforced by EU regulation. Free after registration with a documented REST API plus 2011-2014 historicals. This is the go-to source for placing data-centre load against grid generation mix in Europe (Ireland, the Netherlands, the Nordics). Limit: TSO-level resolution, so distribution-level data-centre demand must come from national regulators instead.

title: U.S. EIA Hourly Electric Grid Monitor (Form EIA-930 data)
institution: U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA)
access: free web dashboard + free API key (EIA API v2, dataset electricity/rto) + bulk CSVs
verification: Official Data.gov announcement of the tool read at origin 2026-11-05: data from 'Form EIA-930, Hourly and Daily Balancing Authority Operations Report' covering 'the 65 electricity balancing authorities that operate the electric grid in the Lower 48 states'; hourly demand, forecast demand, net generation and interchange, plus 'hourly electricity generation by energy source and hourly subregional demand'; flows with Canada and Mexico; released 20 November 2019. The EIA dashboard itself is a JS app that rendered only navigation to the fetcher; July 2018 data start and API endpoints per WebSearch corroborations (data.gov notice; Form EIA-930 descriptions).
relevance: Hourly demand, forecast demand, generation by energy source and interchanges for all 65 Lower-48 balancing authorities - the primary open series for quantifying new data-centre load on US grids such as PJM or ERCOT. Free with an API key (EIA API v2, electricity/rto) plus bulk CSV downloads, maintained by the national statistics agency. Widely used in the Federal Reserve's and LBNL's AI-buildout analyses. Limits: hourly resolution and balancing-authority geography; data-centre-specific electricity sales need newer EIA collections.

title: Electricity Maps data portal - historical carbon intensity and grid-mix signals per zone
date: ongoing (up to about a decade of history per zone)
institution: Electricity Maps ApS, Copenhagen, Denmark
access: free CSV downloads for historical sustainability signals (Carbon Intensity, Carbon-Free Energy %, Renewable Energy %); academic access programme; full power-market signals and forecasts commercial
verification: Metadata only (lead): electricitymaps.com/data-portal 308-redirected to app.electricitymaps.com/datasets, which rendered only the JS map shell (14-day API trial notice, links to 'Data coverage' and Methodology) on 2026-11-05. Per WebSearch corroborations of help.electricitymaps.com and electricitymaps.com/data: free CSV downloads limited to historical Carbon Intensity, Carbon-Free Energy % and Renewable Energy %; 'up to a decade' of history; academic free-access article exists; extended power-market signals and forecasts require a licence; visualisation code open source on GitHub.
relevance: Hourly carbon-intensity and grid-mix signals for 200+ country zones worldwide - the standard way to attach carbon accounting to data-centre and AI-inference siting studies. Free CSVs cover historical sustainability signals (carbon intensity, carbon-free and renewable percentages) with up to a decade of history, plus an academic access programme; full hourly power-market data and forecasts are commercial. Denmark-based maintainer with openly documented methodology. Limits: zone-level, not facility-level, and the free tier excludes prices and forecasts.

title: Singapore Energy Statistics (EMA) - electricity demand and supply data tables for a dense data-centre market
institution: Energy Market Authority (EMA), Singapore
access: free download; additional EMA datasets mirrored free on data.gov.sg
verification: Metadata only (lead): ema.gov.sg returned an empty page to WebFetch and chapter pages were blocked by Incapsula WAF on 2026-11-05. Per WebSearch corroborations: Singapore Energy Statistics is EMA's official publication with an Energy Snapshot, key energy highlights with interactive charts, and 'downloadable data tables'; supplemented by 28 EMA datasets on data.gov.sg (e.g. household electricity consumption by dwelling type).

Free, published by the national energy regulator, with additional machine-readable EMA datasets on data.gov.sg. Useful for learners studying how a small grid governs hyperscale demand. The site's WAF blocked automated reading at check time, so fetch tables manually.

title: USPTO Artificial Intelligence Patent Dataset (AIPD 2023)
authors: Veljko Giczy, Marco Pairolero, Andrew Toole (USPTO Office of the Chief Economist)
institution: U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, Office of the Chief Economist
access: free download (Stata .dta and CSV/TSV) via USPTO Open Data Portal and bulk data directory
verification: AIPD page read at origin 2026-11-05: identifies which of '15.4 million U.S. patent documents (patents and pre-grant publications, or PGPubs) published from 1976 through 2023 contain SI'; machine-learning methodology 'incorporating BERT for Patents'; files ai_model_predictions (DTA 649 MB / CSV 764 MB) and ai_model_training_doc_seedgroups; AIPD 2023 updated 8 January 2025 to fix predict93* threshold variables (89.93% used instead of 93%); citations requested: Pairolero et al. 2025 (Journal of Technology Transfer) and Giczy, Pairolero & Toole 2022.
relevance: A machine-learning-labelled flag set identifying AI ('super intelligence') content across 15.4 million US patent documents from 1976-2023, including pre-grant publications and AI component/subcomponent breakdowns - the public standard for measuring AI inventive activity. Free bulk files in Stata/CSV from the USPTO Open Data Portal, maintained by the Office of the Chief Economist. Use it to track who patents AI, in which technologies, and how the 2023 variables were corrected in January 2025. Limits: US patents only, and labels are model predictions rather than legal determinations.

title: AI Index underlying data and charts (Stanford HAI)
authors: Stanford HAI AI Index Steering Committee (incl. Ray Perrault, Erik Brynjolfsson, Jack Clark)
institution: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI)
access: free - public data and high-resolution chart images released via Google Drive per report; Kaggle mirrors exist
verification: AI Index main page read at origin 2026-11-05: mission 'to provide unbiased, rigorously vetted, and globally sourced data for policymakers, researchers, journalists, executives, and the general public'; annual reports since 2017 with the 2026 edition current; 'Global AI Vibrancy Tool' linked; 2026 report notes 'data transparency is declining'. The report PDF's note that 'raw data and charts: the public data and high-resolution images of all the charts in the report are available on Google Drive' per WebSearch corroborations, plus a Kaggle mirror (AI Index Report 2025). The dedicated /data page returned 404.
relevance: The downloadable spreadsheet and charts layer behind the field's most-cited annual report: R&D and private investment tracking, industry-vs-academia trends, benchmark history, and the annual public-opinion chapter, released as public data with Kaggle mirrors. Produced by Stanford HAI with an academic-industry steering committee; free, though the team itself warns that 'data transparency is declining' across sources. Ideal for building country and time-series comparisons without re-collecting primary data. Limits: access is via report pages and Drive links (the /data page 404'd at check time), and indicator definitions change between editions.

title: Speedtest by Ookla Global Fixed and Mobile Network Performance Maps (Open Data Program)
date: quarterly aggregates from Q1 2019 to present
institution: Ookla (hosted in AWS Registry of Open Data)
access: free anonymous S3 download (--no-sign-request); CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; Shapefile and Parquet
verification: AWS Registry entry read at origin 2026-11-05: 'Global fixed broadband and mobile (cellular) network performance, allocated to zoom level 16 web mercator tiles' (~610.8 m at the equator); download/upload speed and latency 'collected via the Speedtest by Ookla applications' and 'averaged for each tile', GPS-quality results only; quarterly; licence 'CC BY-NC-SA 4.0'; S3 bucket ookla-open-data browsable anonymously. GitHub docs read at origin: variables avg_d_kbps, avg_u_kbps, avg_lat_ms, tests, devices, quadkey; aggregates 'start in Q1 2019'; data 'subject to be reaggregated regularly' to honour DSAR requests.
relevance: Crowdsourced speedtest measurements aggregated to ~610 m tiles globally and quarterly since Q1 2019, with download/upload speeds, latency, test counts and unique devices - the best open proxy for where fixed and mobile network capacity actually exists. Free anonymous S3 access under CC BY-NC-SA, in Shapefile and Parquet. Use it to map AI-connectivity gaps, i.e., which regions could realistically consume frontier AI services or host remote work. Limits: non-commercial licence, bias toward Speedtest users, and tiles are reaggregated for privacy.

title: RIA ICT Access and Usage Survey (After Access series) - household/individual microdata for African countries
date: 2007/08 and 2011/12 waves; 2017/18 After Access wave (latest released microdata)
institution: Research ICT Africa, Cape Town; distributed via DataFirst, University of Cape Town (mirrored on World Bank Microdata Library)
access: microdata 'licensed use files, available with restrictions' (registration via DataFirst); questionnaires and documentation free
verification: World Bank Microdata catalog entry read at origin 2026-11-05 (AFR_2017_RIAS_v01_M): 'Household and Individual ICT Access and Usage Survey 2017-2018' produced by RIA, 'a non-profit, public interest, research entity'; 13 countries listed (Botswana, Cameroon, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria, Rwanda, Tunisia, Tanzania, Uganda, South Africa); 'nationally representative on a household and individual level for individuals 16 years of age or older'; 16 questionnaire modules incl. mobile money, internet and social media use; 'Licensed use files, available with restrictions'; DOI 10.25828/kcsd-nb04; distributor DataFirst, UCT. RIA's 2019 announcement points to DataFirst for download.
relevance: The longest-running multi-country ICT access and usage microdata series in Africa, covering mobile ownership, internet use, mobile money and electricity access across 13+ countries, nationally representative at household and individual level. Produced by Research ICT Africa and distributed as licensed (restricted) files through DataFirst at the University of Cape Town, mirrored on the World Bank Microdata Library; questionnaires are free, microdata needs registration. Baseline for studying who in Africa can participate in the AI economy - though the released wave predates generative AI, so pair with newer rounds.

title: APJII Survei Penetrasi Internet Indonesia - annual Indonesia internet penetration survey archive
date: annual series (release-year archive available on portal)
institution: APJII (Indonesian Internet Service Providers Association), Jakarta
access: free report downloads (Indonesian language)

relevance: The reference annual survey for internet penetration, device use and demographics in Indonesia - Southeast Asia's largest internet market - with official reports downloadable by release year from APJII's survey portal. Free (Indonesian-language) and produced by the ISP association, making it the de facto national source cited in Indonesian digital policy. Useful for grounding AI-access discussions in SEA's largest market. Limits: methodology and sample details live inside each report PDF, and the portal page itself exposes only the archive, so download the year's report to verify figures.

title: IndicVoices - open speech dataset for 22 scheduled Indian languages
date: 2024 (ACL Findings, arXiv:2403.01926); dataset card updated 23 December 2025
institution: AI4Bharat, Indian Institute of Technology Madras (funded by Bhashini/MeitY and Nilekani Philanthropies)
access: gated Hugging Face download (login + conditions, HF access token); CC BY 4.0
verification: HF dataset card read at origin 2026-11-05: 'a total of 23.7K hours' of speech with '11.2K hours have already been transcribed'; 51K speakers across 400+ Indian districts; 22 scheduled Indian languages; natural speech split read 8% / extempore 76% / conversational 15%; licence CC BY 4.0; gated access with token; full-length audio 745 GB via tgz archives from an E2E Networks object store; open-source collection blueprint shared. The ai4bharat.iitm.ac.in datasets page currently shows only a banner that datasets are moving to HuggingFace.
relevance: One of the largest open speech corpora for a Global South language family: 23,700 hours collected from 51,000 speakers in 400+ Indian districts across 22 scheduled languages, with an open blueprint for replicating the collection pipeline. Built by AI4Bharat at IIT Madras under MeitY's Bhashini programme; CC BY 4.0 but gated (login plus conditions). Central for learners studying how multilingual data underpins inclusive AI - it powers IndicASR covering all 22 languages. Limits: transcription still catching up (11.2K of 23.7K hours) and the full download is heavy (745 GB).
